1.open: Think of something you learned slowly over time, like a skill, a recipe or a language. What helped you keep going?
questions: Peter writes to ordinary believers who have "received a faith as precious as ours" (v. 1). How does it land to hear that your faith is just as valuable as an apostle's?

Verse 3 says God's divine power "has given us everything we need for life and godliness." What is the difference between hearing that you already have what you need and feeling that you are still missing something?

In verse 4 we are told we may "become partakers of the divine nature." Many read this as becoming more like God in goodness, not becoming God. What do you think growing like God looks like in daily life?
Peter says to "make every effort" to add goodness, knowledge, self-control and more to our faith (v. 5). Which quality on his list feels hardest for you right now, and what makes it hard?
The list ends with love (v. 7). Why might Peter place love last? What changes if the other qualities are missing it?

Verse 9 describes someone who is "nearsighted to the point of blindness, having forgotten that he has been cleansed from his past sins." How does remembering forgiveness help us grow, rather than just trying harder?

In verse 10 Peter urges believers to "make your calling and election sure." Christians differ on whether this means our effort helps secure salvation or only confirms what God has already secured. How does each reading shape the way you hear the verse?

Peter says the message is not "cleverly devised fables" but is based on eyewitnesses of Jesus' majesty (v. 16). If you have doubts or questions about whether this is true, what are they, and what would help you most?
1.life: Pick one quality from Peter's list in verses 5 to 7. This week, take one small, specific step toward it, and each evening remind yourself that God has already given you what you need to grow.
1.prayer: Thank God for giving us everything we need through knowing him. Ask for patience in the slow work of growing, and for love to shape all of it.
1.tip: Verses 5 to 11 can sound like a to-do list that earns God's favor. Point the group back to verses 3 and 4 and verse 9, where growth rests on what God has already given and forgiven. On verse 10, say plainly that Christians read it differently, and don't try to settle it.

2.open: Have you ever bought something, or fallen for a pitch, that promised a lot and turned out to be empty? What happened?
questions: Peter says false teachers "will secretly introduce destructive heresies" (v. 1). Why do you think the most harmful teaching often arrives quietly rather than loudly?
Verse 3 says that "in their greed, these false teachers will exploit you with deceptive words." What are some ways money or personal gain can bend what people say about God, then and now?
Peter gives three examples from the past: the angels, the flood and Sodom and Gomorrah (vv. 4-6). What do you think he wanted his first readers to take from them?

In two of those examples God also rescued someone. Verse 9 says, "the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials." What does it mean to you that rescue is part of this chapter and not only judgment?
Lot lived among people whose conduct distressed him "day after day" (v. 8). Have you ever felt worn down by the world around you? How did you cope, or how are you coping?
Peter says these teachers "promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity" (v. 19). How can you tell the difference between real freedom and a different kind of trap?

Verses 20 to 22 are sobering, and Christians read them differently: some see believers who fell away, others see people who never truly believed. However you read it, what does the passage stir up in you? If it makes you anxious about your own faith, say so honestly.
Peter writes this so believers will stay alert and grounded. What practical habits help you notice when something you hear sounds good but pulls you away from Jesus?
2.life: This week, when you hear a teaching, a podcast or advice that promises freedom or an easier way, stop and ask three questions: What does this say about Jesus? Who gains from it? Where does it lead? Talk it over with a friend in the group.
2.prayer: Thank God that he knows how to rescue his people. Ask for wisdom to tell what is true from what is merely attractive, and pray for anyone in the group who feels unsteady in their faith.
2.tip: This chapter is harsh in tone, and some people will worry about whether they have 'fallen away' (vv. 20 to 22). Say plainly that Christians read those verses differently, and that Peter is warning about teachers who lead others astray, not trying to frighten sincere people who struggle. Make room for anyone who wants to talk about their doubts, and avoid pointing at specific people or churches as false teachers.

3.open: What is something you have waited a long time for, and how did the waiting feel?
questions: The writer says his letters are "reminders to stir you to wholesome thinking" (v. 1). What helps you remember what matters when life gets noisy?
Scoffers ask, "Where is the promise of His coming?" (v. 4). What does their question sound like today, and when have you caught yourself asking something like it?
The writer answers that "with the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day" (v. 8). What do you make of that? Does it comfort you, frustrate you, or a bit of both?
Verse 9 says the Lord "is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance." How does it change the way you see the waiting to think of it as patience?
The day of the Lord will "come like a thief" (v. 10). What do you think it means to live ready without living in fear?
Verse 11 asks, "what kind of people ought you to be?" and verse 13 describes a "new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells." How might hope for that world shape an ordinary Tuesday?
Christians read the fire of verses 10 to 12 differently: some think this world is replaced, others that it is cleansed and renewed. Why might it matter, or not matter, which view we hold?

The chapter ends with "grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ" (v. 18). Where do you feel you are growing, and where do you feel stuck or even doubtful? Be as honest as you like.
3.life: Think of one person you have given up on or stopped praying for. This week, pray for them each day, asking God to be as patient with them as he has been with you. If it fits, reach out with a kind word or message.
3.prayer: Thank God for his patience with you and with the people you love. Ask for honest hearts about doubt and waiting, and for the grace to keep growing while you wait.
3.tip: Verses 10 to 12 can pull the group into debates about the end times. Name the disagreement in one line, then steer back to verse 9 and verse 11: God's patience and how we live while we wait. If someone voices doubt that Jesus will return, thank them for saying it and let them know the first readers asked the same question.
